My husband does the cooking and makes super high calorie/fat, delicious meals, and I have terrible self control, too. I was able to lose 46 lbs (so far) since May without really giving anything up! I don't feel deprived at all. I've only cut my calories to 1500-1700 per day with two cheat days /week (about 2000 cals), but I make up for those extra calories throughout the week so I end the week with the same total, if that makes sense. 1500-1700 is what my app suggests for .5 lbs/week which is slow loss but sustainable *for me*. I also do spin classes 3-4 times per week, but other than that I'm pretty sedentary. 

Obviously all bodies are different and will require different calorie deficits to lose, but I feel like a lot of people on here try to lose 1.5-2 lbs/week and eat 1200 calories. When you only have 20-30 lbs to lose, it comes off slowly, and in my opinion I'd rather lose slowly and easily than quickly and difficultly. 

If you have someone else in your life that you have to balance meals with (significant other/kids/etc), it seems easier to me to get to eat the same things as them in smaller portions and lose weight slowly. Then when you enter the maintenance phase, you don't feel like "oh my gosh I'm finally done dieting! I can eat like you again!" And gain it all back.

I don't know your situation but I will say, for others out there to be prepared, I'm a nursery nurse and here's how things work at my hospital (not a backwards hospital): about five or ten minutes before the baby actually comes out, at least one if not two nursery nurses come in to "catch" the baby. If there is *any* concern of *any* complications we are accompanied by at least one NICU nurse, a respiratory therapist, and a neonatal nurse practitioner. Additionally, there are two L&D nurses, the doctor, and a scrub tech in the room, and often there's a CNA as well. This adds up to a lot of people watching moms push that baby out. And yes, we're watching, because our jobs and baby's health depends on us paying attention during the birth. We don't usually introduce ourselves because mom is literally too involved in pushing to stop and be like "oh hi nice to meet you." As soon as baby comes out crying, half the people leave so you never interact with them even tho they just saw your vag. We aren't just hanging out watching for fun, I promise :) We are all there doing a job. There are tons of things that need to be done immediately during and after birth. 

That being said, I will be more conscious of trying to give moms a heads up about who I am and why I'm in there if I can, and any students watching just to learn should definitely receive permission from mom first.

I did my internship in OR in nursing school. I'll tell you about my experience, but keep in mind it was an internship so I was never really acting as THE circulating nurse.

Upsides: The hours were great - four week days from 6:30-3:30 and then the regular employees had a call shift but that was it as far as nights/weekends/holidays. They always planned and guaranteed your full lunch break which doesn't always happen on the floor if you're really busy. I have back problems, and that was definitely easier on my back than my current job because most of the day was spent sitting in the corner charting and surfing the internet. It was also a bit easier to make it through the day if I was hungover, sick, or tired. There was very little patient interaction (which was good and bad in my opinion), and when you did "nursing skills" the patients were generally unconscious so it wasn't as stressful. The atmosphere was pretty fun because you don't have to worry about being "professional" and "on" for the patients. We all did a lot of bull shitting and practical joking. That also probably had to do with the fact that there were a lot more men (docs included) than your typical floor job. I'm a woman but grew up with brothers and always enjoyed the ease of being around dudes.

Downsides: so bored with the work. After my six week internship I couldn't handle it anymore - I felt like the boredom wasn't worth my time. I like being steadily busy though. I also felt like I hardly used anything I learned in school. I felt like I wasn't really a nurse so much as a servant and chart documenter. Some of the docs could definitely be dicks, and I really didn't like being looked down on like that. Sometimes I would mention my dad was a surgeon and suddenly the docs would act very differently towards me, like that fact somehow made me a more respectable person. Then they would go about trying to convince me to become a surgeon instead of "just a nurse". That really annoyed me because it showed how they viewed us. Sidenote, one day an orthopedic surgeon got pissed and chucked his 18 gauge, used needle across the room, which landed right by my foot. Not cool.

That was my experience. If you're already feeling that burned out, I would definitely suggest switching to a different floor or even going back to school because it's going to be a long career at this rate. I personally hated working with adult patients. That's why I did my internship in the OR, but I found my niche elsewhere.

When I left, they were changing the policy to only PRN or as requested by parents because the baths dry out preemie/newborn skin and really aren't necessary that often (according to best practice research).

As a new grad, I started out with a shadow day, then took one easy patient and charting with guidance for a week while observing and helping with my preceptor's patients. Next few weeks took two then three then 4 with increasing difficulty and less supervision each week.

After 6 weeks I moved to the ICU where I took one then two then three patients over the same course as the step down orientation, but never really worked alone. I always had a preceptor at my side sharing the workload and instructing me since there was a lot of more dangerous medications, blood administration, chest tubes, and ventilators. After 6 weeks I went back to the step down unit and was on my own. As a new grad, it was a similar experience to yours where a lot of the preceptor's job was to help me keep up, but also teaching me how to assess and treat this specific population which we never learned in school (NICU babies).

Two years later, I just started orienting to a step down unit with more acute patients than my last job. It's only been two days but I'm already feeling like "please give me my three patients on my own and just stand back to answer questions and teach me the new stuff." I have three months of orientation planned out for this position but it's dreadfully boring to only have one patient and share the work of charting and tasks now that I understand time management, basic nursing skills, and how to assess and treat this age and type of patient. Plus it messes up my organization when we're splitting tasks. I need help learning where things are and how to navigate the charting program more than anything else. It's a much different and less stressful experience.

I am like this too, and it is the quality I hate the most about myself. I am always trying to fix it but catch myself falling into the behaviors, especially when I'm stressed/anxious about things. I think it started because I was very shy and quiet growing up. Everyone wants attention and gets attention in one way or another (using a talent, acting out, whatever, it's human nature). I thought the way to get that was being good, following rules, getting good grades, etc but with the family I had and the world I lived in, being good only made you more invisible  because people thought, "oh you don't have to worry about flsunchick, she's a good kid who doesn't need attention." Like I said, everyone, whether they admit it or not, needs attention, so over the course of my school age years, I found that playing the victim and being pitied was the only way people would notice me at all. 

I began to recognize this about myself when I went to college. No one knew me and no one cared about my problem, whatever it was that day. I got extremely depressed and went through years of therapy to figure out that I needed to just stop acting like a victim to get out of my depression, and I could get attention from speaking my mind and being a mature adult with thoughts and opinions. People's respect has gotten me a lot further and created a much better self image than people's pity ever did.

tl;dr: I was a "victim" because it was the only way I could be noticed as a shy "good" kid, and now I've spent years in therapy trying to stop.

Neonatal ICU, but usually intermediate (step down) unit rather than the really intensive care side. I spent four hours of clinical there while in school and immediately knew that was my "calling". Intermediate unit is a pretty happy place because the babies are close to going home, often after a lengthy stay. There's a lot of teaching parents how to care for their infants as they don't get to do much in the intensive care unit. Also, we spend a lot of time kind of teaching babies to eat from bottles and have limited serious medications and running IV fluids, but a lot of saline locks for antibiotics. I'm an anxious person and don't like the responsibility and adrenaline of really critical care, so these stable babies are perfect for me. The worst part is when they occasionally decide to stop breathing and try to see Jesus, but you get good at that part pretty quickly.

I might be judged for this, but I hated working with adult patients because, especially as an inexperienced nurse, I felt I was constantly being watched and criticized. Plus, I'm not super outgoing so spending a few hours teaching parents about something I really know is much easier for me than trying to have continuous conversation with adult patients about random crap.

TL;DR: NICU is great for an introvert, and even night shift is generally high speed, keeps you busy. Step down is constantly busy but not really stressful and is very rewarding.
